---
title: "Interpreting the results"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
link-citations: true
---

Climate projections can be overlaid in the same stressor space after vulnerabilities have been mapped.
Their position helps assess whether concerning conditions are consistent with available climate evidence.
Reference periods, seasons and spatial scales must be comparable for that overlay to be meaningful.
The fraction of projections in a vulnerable region is not automatically a probability of future failure;
such an interpretation requires additional assumptions about the ensemble and its sampling [@brown2012].

Repeating the experiment for alternative infrastructure designs or operating policies shows how each
option changes the vulnerable region.
This supports the search for **robust** options that perform acceptably across a range of futures.
It also helps identify where additional information, monitoring or a more detailed assessment could
change a decision [@fowler2024].

The findings remain conditional on the chosen stressors, ranges, models and performance criteria.
A temperature–precipitation surface cannot reveal the effects of changing drought persistence or demand
unless these are represented in the experiment.
Weather generation must be checked against the characteristics that matter to the system, and model
performance under unfamiliar conditions remains uncertain.
A stress test therefore provides evidence about sensitivities, failure conditions and adaptation options;
it does not predict a unique future or establish safety against every possible stress [@fowler2024].
